extracted.intended_audience: expert adult audience, including professional development and academic researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and mechanisms by which market forces (audience demand, advertisers, costs, competition, ownership) shape which stories become news across print, television, and the Internet, and policy levers to alter that outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether a story appears (determinants of appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a story appears in print, on television, or on the Internet depends on who is interested, its value to advertisers, the costs of assembling the details, and competitors' products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four factors (audience interest, advertiser value, newsgathering cost, competitor offerings) as primary evaluative criteria when predicting or judging coverage decisions; examples and empirical analysis across media markets are provided in the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience interest / matching to viewer preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: News choices are shaped by what specific audiences prefer — e.g., younger audiences prefer sports to international news, health and lifestyle to government news, and more conflict and less exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news by how well it targets and matches the preferences of demographic segments; the book uses surveys and ratings to demonstrate audience-driven content shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value to advertisers / profitability incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of a story to advertisers influences whether it will be selected and emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider advertisers' willingness to pay and how that translates into editorial selection pressure; profitable (or advertiser-friendly) topics are more likely to receive coverage or favorable framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of assembling details / newsgathering costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The costs of assembling the details of a story affect whether outlets will pursue it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that are inexpensive to produce (e.g., repackaged content, wire copy, celebrity pieces) are more likely to be chosen than those requiring costly investigation; factor cost when judging coverage gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition and product differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitors' products and competitive pressures (e.g., cable competition, deregulation, ownership changes) encourage shifts in the type of news presented, such as moving from hard political news toward softer entertainment-focused stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how market structure and rival offerings drive editorial choices and format changes; competitive dynamics can incentivize niche targeting and sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from hard news to soft/news as entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Market incentives have encouraged a shift from hard news about politics toward more soft news about entertainers, celebrity profiles, human-interest stories, and product hype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating newsroom quality or public-service value, measure the balance between substantive hard news and soft, entertainment-oriented content and note how incentives favor the latter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution of partisanship and nonpartisan reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and market forces explain changes in press independence and partisanship (e.g., newspapers 1870–1900 evolved toward nonpartisan reporting; later partisan elements reemerged when outlets targeted specific audiences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical patterns and institutional incentives to evaluate claims of media bias or independence; consider how audience targeting can revive partisan slants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy levers to increase supply of hard news
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton calls for lower costs of access to government information, a greater role for nonprofits in funding journalism, development of norms that stress hard news reporting, and defining digital and Internet property rights to encourage the flow of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as actionable criteria or interventions for policymakers and funders seeking to alter media incentives: reduce information-access costs, support nonprofit funding, cultivate hard-news norms, and clarify digital property rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists as market goods (incentives for reporters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists themselves are treated as goods shaped by market incentives—factors such as reputation, salary, brand, and marketability influence journalistic behavior and content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate newsroom staffing and reporter incentives (career concerns, reputation effects, pay structures) as part of understanding why certain content is produced or avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-type selection (hard news vs human-interest, celebrity, product hype)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different content types (hard political reporting, human-interest stories, celebrity profiles, product hype) are differentially favored by market incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify and compare content types when assessing news quality or market effects; note which types are promoted by audience and advertiser demand versus those that serve public-interest information needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical measures (ratings, surveys, statistical significance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical measures such as Nielsen ratings, surveys, and statistical analysis determine and demonstrate how audiences consume news and how markets shape content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on audience metrics and rigorous statistical evidence to evaluate claims about news selection and to quantify shifts between hard and soft news; the book provides examples and charts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest vs willingness to pay (rational ignorance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public's limited willingness to pay and rational ignorance about some topics affects the supply of public-interest news; if consumers don't demand it, markets underprovide it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the adequacy of news provision, consider demand-side failures (low willingness to pay) and externalities that justify policy or nonprofit interventions to support public-interest reporting.
